sections.h: Jeremiah in the last siege (chapters 32 to 38)
sections.b: In the last two years of Judah's kingdom Jeremiah was arrested for treason, locked in a cistern-dungeon, beaten, and held in the palace courtyard. In that courtyard he bought a field, prayed, received the promise of an everlasting covenant and sent his scribe Baruch to read a scroll. The stories of chapters 36 to 38 show a prophet who is neither a traitor nor a hero by his own account, but a man who says the same thing to every king: surrender and live.

Three covenants meet in these chapters. The LORD promises an everlasting covenant in which he will never stop doing good to his people and will put the fear of him in their hearts (32:38–41). He ties his covenants with David and the Levites to his covenant with day and night (33:20–26). And the people of Jerusalem cut a covenant to release their slaves and break it, so that the LORD treats them as the calf they cut in two (34:8–22; compare Genesis 15).

sections.h: The promise to David in Jeremiah 33
sections.b: Jeremiah 33:14–26 says that David will never lack a man on his throne and that the Levite priests will never lack a man to offer sacrifices, as sure as day and night. The passage is not in the oldest Greek. Jews read it of a future king, Christians of Jesus, and critical scholars of the hope of the Persian period.

Jeremiah 33:15–16 repeats the promise of 23:5–6 with small changes: a Branch of righteousness sprouts for David, and the name "The LORD is our righteousness" is given to the city. The Targum reads the Branch as the Messiah.

Jeremiah's purchase of a field (32:6–15), the promise that fields will again be bought (32:43–44) and the return of the voices of bride and groom (33:10–11) are signs given before the exile that it will end. They sit beside the letter to the exiles (29:5) and the promise to turn the fortunes of Judah and Israel (33:7).

sections.h: The release of Hebrew slaves under siege
sections.b: In Zedekiah's reign the people of Jerusalem freed their Hebrew slaves in a covenant before the LORD, then took them back when the siege lifted. Jeremiah calls this a profaning of the LORD's name and a breaking of the covenant at the exodus (34:8–22). The laws behind it are Exodus 21:2, Deuteronomy 15:12–18 and Leviticus 25:39–46.

The Hebrew deror, "release," is the word of Leviticus 25:10 and Isaiah 61:1. Zedekiah's release of the slaves is the one place where a king and people try to keep it, and the LORD turns the word against them: he proclaims a "release" to the sword, the plague and the famine (34:17).

sections.h: The Messiah in the Targum of Jeremiah 33:15
sections.b: The Aramaic Targum of Jeremiah renders the Branch of 33:15 as "Messiah of righteousness." Radak, in the Middle Ages, connects the name "The LORD is our righteousness" (33:16) to Jerusalem and also to the Messiah. Christian readers see Jesus.

Jehudi, who reads the scroll to the king, is a great-grandson of a man named Cushi (36:14), and Ebed-melech the Cushite rescues Jeremiah from the cistern (38:7–13). His reward is told in 39:15–18. A foreigner and court official acts where the officials of Judah do not.

Jeremiah's cousin Hanamel offers him the field at Anathoth because the right of redemption is his (32:7–8). The law is Leviticus 25:25, and the case of Ruth 4 shows it at work. Jeremiah's purchase is a family redemption done as a promise to the nation.

sections.h: Topheth and the high places of Baal (Jeremiah 32:35)
sections.b: Jeremiah 32:35 charges Judah with building the high places of Baal in the Valley of Ben-hinnom "to make their sons and their daughters pass over to Molech," a thing that the LORD says never came into his heart. The Greek calls the god "Molech the king."

sections.h: The Levite priests who will never be lacking
sections.b: Jeremiah 33:18 and 33:21–22 promise that the Levite priests will never lack a man to offer sacrifices and will be as many as the stars. Catholic, Orthodox, Reformed and Dispensationalist readers disagree on how the promise is met (see the card at Jeremiah 33).

sections.h: A king asks a prophet to pray
sections.b: Zedekiah sends two men to ask Jeremiah to pray for the city (37:3), though the LORD had told Jeremiah not to pray for this people (7:16; 11:14; 14:11). The request is made and not answered as the king hoped.

sections.h: Jeremiah 33:14–26 and other passages the Greek lacks
sections.b: The Greek of Jeremiah lacks 33:14–26 and parts of 32:5, 32:11 and 38:7, and has a different sense at 34:18, 36:25 and 38:9. A Qumran scroll, 4QJer-c, has words of 33:16–20 in the longer (Masoretic) form. See the variants at each verse.

Chapters 32 to 38 show the test of Deuteronomy 18:22 in a siege. Jeremiah knows a word is from the LORD when his cousin comes as promised (32:8). In 37:19 he asks the king where the prophets are who said Babylon would not come. The chapters also show a prophecy that Zedekiah would "die in peace" (34:5) that is hard to square with his blinding.

In prison Jeremiah asks King Zedekiah, "Where are your prophets who prophesied to you that the king of Babylon will not come against you?" The test is Deuteronomy 18:22: a prophet whose word does not come true has not spoken for the LORD.

sections.h: A fast in the ninth month
sections.b: In the ninth month of Jehoiakim's fifth year (December 604 BC) the people of Jerusalem and Judah proclaimed a fast, and Baruch read the scroll in the temple (36:9). A public fast was a call to turn back and ask God for mercy in a crisis.

The Rechabites refused wine because their ancestor Jonadab had commanded it (35:5–10). The LORD praises their obedience to their ancestor, not the rule itself, and the story has often been misused to teach that all wine is forbidden.

Jeremiah's chapters 32 to 38 give the fullest account of the last king of Judah: locked-up prophet and secret meetings (37:17; 38:14), a king who will not listen but cannot stop listening, a king afraid of his officials (38:5). He is told twice that he will be taken to Babylon, and offered a way out (38:17–18).

sections.h: Baruch the scribe in Jeremiah 32 and 36
sections.b: Baruch son of Neriah first appears as keeper of the field deed (32:12) and then as the writer and reader of Jeremiah's scroll (36:4–19). A clay seal impression naming Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe was published in 1978; it is unprovenanced and its authenticity is debated.

Jehoiakim cut up and burned Jeremiah's scroll in the ninth month (winter) of 604 BC and ordered the arrest of Jeremiah and Baruch (36:22–26). He was told that none of his line would sit on David's throne and that his body would be thrown out in the heat and frost (36:30).

Pharaoh Hophra's army came out of Egypt about 588 BC and the Babylonians lifted the siege for a time. Jeremiah said the Egyptians would go home (37:7). The Egyptian help had failed the kingdom before (Isaiah 30:1–7).

sections.h: The guilt of the fathers in Jeremiah 32:18
sections.b: Jeremiah's prayer quotes the saying that God "repays the guilt of the fathers into the laps of their children after them" (32:18; Exodus 34:7), while chapter 31 promises that each will die for his own guilt (31:29–30). The book holds both: the city pays for generations of sin and the new covenant ends the proverb.

Jeremiah sinks in the mud of a cistern (38:6) and is rescued by Ebed-melech. The scene echoes Joseph's pit (Genesis 37:24) and the laments of the psalms, and readers have set it beside Lamentations 3:53–55.

The Rechabites were a clan of Kenite descent who followed the rules of their ancestor Jonadab son of Rechab: no wine, no houses, no fields, but tents. Jeremiah used their obedience to shame Judah's disobedience (35:1–19).

These chapters are set inside the last siege, from the winter of 589/588 to the summer of 586: a tenth year of Zedekiah in 32:1, the lifting of the siege in 37:5, hunger in 37:21 and 38:9, and the capture in 38:28. Lachish and Azekah are the last fortified towns (34:7).
